topic: Who signs a system card before production release
stem: An internal standard requires a system card to be signed before an AI system is released to production. Who should sign it?

options.text: The accountable owner of the use case, since the card is a set of assertions somebody has to stand behind.
The engineering lead who built the system, as the person with the most detailed knowledge of how it actually behaves.
The chair of the AI governance board, as the representative of the body that approved the deployment into production.
The organisation's data protection officer, as the reviewer of the data classes the system processes and retains.

explanation.correct: A signature on a card is a claim that its contents are true and that someone will answer for them. Only the accountable owner is in a position to make that claim across the whole card — approved scope, data reached, evaluation evidence, oversight arrangement — and only the owner has the authority to act if any of it turns out to be wrong. Signing also creates the right incentive: an owner who must personally assert that the evaluation covers the intended population reads the evaluation before signing.

distractors.B: The engineering lead is the right author for most of the technical content and should certainly contribute. Authorship is not accountability, and an engineer cannot commit the organisation to the approved scope or to the oversight arrangement that sits outside the code.
distractors.C: The board's role is to approve, and its approval is recorded separately. Having the chair sign the card conflates the decision to permit the system with the assertion that its description is accurate, and the chair has no basis for the second.
distractors.D: Data protection review is one input to the card and typically produces its own record. Signing the whole card would require the officer to assert things about evaluation coverage and operational oversight that fall outside their remit.

explanation.concept: The system card is signed by the person accountable for the use case, because a card is a set of assertions and assertions need someone answerable for them. Contributors author sections; the approval body records approval separately; the owner signs.
explanation.tip: Distinguish author, approver and signer. Governance items frequently offer the person who knows most and the person who approved as decoys for the person who is accountable.

topic: Managing model provider concentration across an AI estate
stem: A Nigerian retail bank has nine registered AI use cases, all running on a single model provider through one gateway; two of them support regulated customer communications and two are used inside the branch network's daily operating process. The board's operational resilience standard requires the bank to identify and plan for the loss of any single critical supplier. The head of architecture proposes maintaining a second provider in parallel for all nine. Which TWO points should shape the response? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Concentration should be managed per use case against its criticality, so that only the uses the bank genuinely cannot operate without justify the cost of a maintained alternative.
Running a second provider in parallel across all nine removes the concentration exposure, because either provider can serve any request at any moment.

Each critical use case needs a rehearsed fallback that does not depend on the provider — including a documented manual or degraded process — since a second model needs its own prompts and evaluation before it can be trusted.
Concentration is addressed through the contract's availability commitments, so the right response is to negotiate stronger service levels rather than to change the architecture.
The gateway rather than the provider is the real single point of failure, so applications should be permitted to call the provider directly as a bypass route when the gateway is unavailable.

explanation.correct: Resilience is bought per use case, not per estate. Two of the nine sit in a daily operating process and two support regulated communications; the rest may be able to stop for a day with no consequence, and paying to maintain a second provider for them is money spent on an exposure the bank does not have. For the ones that do matter, the honest planning assumption is that a second model is not a drop-in: it needs its own prompts, its own evaluation and its own approval before anyone should route live traffic to it. That is why the fallback that has to exist and be rehearsed is the non-AI one.

distractors.B: Maintaining two providers in parallel does not make them interchangeable. Prompts, output shapes and failure modes differ, so the untested provider is a second system the bank has not evaluated — and the belief that failover is instant is precisely what makes the outage worse when it arrives.
distractors.D: Availability commitments allocate money after an outage. They neither prevent one nor keep the branch process running through it, and the standard asks the bank to plan for the loss of the supplier, not to be compensated for it.
distractors.E: Allowing applications to bypass the gateway would dismantle the control point the bank's registration, logging and enforcement all depend on. It trades a resilience concern for a governance failure, and the gateway can be made resilient without opening a bypass.

explanation.concept: Model provider concentration is managed per use case by criticality, and the credible fallback for a critical AI use case is usually a rehearsed degraded or manual process rather than an unevaluated second model. Treat multi-provider capability as an option that still requires its own approval path.
explanation.tip: Resilience items reward proportionality and rehearsal. Options claiming a second supplier eliminates the risk ignore that the alternative is untested until you have tested it.

topic: Human authorisation for an irreversible autonomous action
stem: A Romanian telecommunications operator's Claude-based network operations agent executes remediation runbooks autonomously when its confidence threshold is met. One runbook reroutes traffic away from a regional core node; reversing it takes about forty minutes and the reroute itself briefly degrades service for roughly 90,000 subscribers. The change advisory board wants a control on this specific runbook without removing the agent's autonomy elsewhere. Which control fits?

options.text: Raise the confidence threshold at which the agent will run that runbook so it executes only when highly confident, and log every invocation for review at the weekly operations meeting.
Require the agent to write its reasoning to the operations log immediately before executing, so an operator reading the log afterwards can identify a wrong decision quickly and begin the reversal.
Restrict the runbook to off-peak hours, when the number of subscribers affected by a mistaken reroute would be substantially lower than during the daytime peak.
Require a named on-shift network engineer to authorise this action before it executes, with the agent's reasoning and the affected node shown at the point of decision.

explanation.correct: Forty minutes to reverse and 90,000 subscribers degraded is a combination that no after-the-fact mechanism helps with — by the time anyone reads a log, the cost has been incurred and cannot be recovered for most of an hour. This is the specific case where autonomy has to yield to authorisation, and the design detail matters: the engineer needs the agent's reasoning and the affected node presented at the moment of decision, or the authorisation degrades into the same reflexive approval that makes human review decorative. The agent keeps its autonomy on the reversible runbooks, which is what the board asked for.

distractors.A: Model confidence is not a calibrated probability of correctness and does not become one at a higher threshold. It also fails on the wrong axis: threshold tuning changes how often the action fires, not what it costs when it fires wrongly.
distractors.B: Logging reasoning before execution improves diagnosis and shortens the reversal, which is worth having. It is a detection improvement applied to an action whose harm lands the instant it executes, so the forty-minute exposure is unchanged.
distractors.C: A time window shrinks the blast radius without adding any control over whether the action is correct. Network incidents do not schedule themselves off-peak, so the restriction either blocks legitimate remediation when it is most needed or gets overridden.

explanation.concept: Scale oversight to reversibility and blast radius, not to how often an action occurs. Where reversal is slow and impact is wide, require named human authorisation at the point of execution with the reasoning presented — and leave autonomy intact for the actions that can simply be undone.
explanation.tip: When a stem gives you a reversal time and an affected population, it is telling you that detection-based answers arrive too late. Look for the option that intervenes before the action.

topic: Controlling AI browser extensions installed by staff
stem: A Hungarian pharmaceutical distributor's IT team discovers that 140 staff have installed browser extensions that summarise or rewrite the current page, several of which request permission to read and change data on all sites. The extensions are free, so nothing appears in spend data, and they authenticate to their own vendors rather than to the corporate identity tenant, so nothing appears in application consent logs. Which TWO controls address this class of use? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Move extension installation to an allow-list managed through enterprise browser policy, so that only reviewed extensions can be installed on managed devices.
Add the vendors' domains to the egress block list, which stops the current extensions working until staff find replacements that are not yet listed.
Inventory the extensions installed across the managed fleet and assess them against the permissions they request, treating broad read-and-change host permissions as the risk driver.
Require staff to declare any browser extension they use in the annual AI self-declaration, so that extension use is reflected in the register alongside other tools.
Raise the frequency of the AI policy reminder email to monthly and name browser extensions explicitly as a prohibited category of tool.

explanation.correct: Extensions evade both of the usual discovery signals, which the stem states explicitly, so the visibility has to come from the endpoint. Enumerating what is installed across the managed fleet and reading the permissions each one requests gives the distributor both the inventory and the risk ranking in one pass — an extension with read-and-change access to all sites can see every page a user opens, including systems holding prescription and customer data. The allow-list is the enforcement half: it makes installation a decision the organisation makes rather than one each user makes, and it holds without anyone remembering a rule.

distractors.B: Domain blocking is a per-vendor game against a category with a very large supply. It also breaks tools without giving the distributor any view of what was installed or what those extensions could read while they were running.
distractors.D: Self-declaration is the mechanism these uses already escaped, and most staff do not think of a browser extension as an AI tool at all. It also runs annually against a population that changes weekly.
distractors.E: Monthly reminders raise awareness and leave 140 installations in place. Nothing in the measure removes an extension, prevents the next installation, or tells the distributor what the existing ones can read.

explanation.concept: Endpoint-resident AI tools leave no spend and no identity trace, so they require endpoint controls: enumerate installed extensions and rank them by the permissions they hold, then move installation to an allow-list. Permission scope, not vendor name, is the risk signal worth acting on.
explanation.tip: When a stem rules out two discovery channels by name, it is telling you which layer the answer lives at. Everything financial and identity-based is already excluded.

topic: Evidence versus attestation when testing an AI control
stem: An assurance team is testing whether an AI governance control operates as designed. What distinguishes evidence from attestation?

options.text: Attestation is given by the control owner, whereas evidence must be produced by a party independent of the first line of defence.
Attestation is a statement that the control operated; evidence is an artefact the control itself produced, which the tester can inspect directly.
Attestation covers a whole period, whereas evidence captures a point in time and must be sampled across the period before it means anything.
Attestation is acceptable for lower-tier controls, whereas evidence is required only for the controls that the annual assurance plan designates as key and tests in depth.

explanation.correct: The difference is whether the tester has to take someone's word for it. An attestation is a claim, and a claim can be sincere and still wrong — the owner may believe the gateway blocks personal data because that is what the design says. Evidence is a by-product of the control operating: the blocked request log, the credential issuance record tied to a register entry, the expired exception that actually lapsed. It exists whether or not anyone remembered the control was there, which is exactly why it can be tested independently.

distractors.A: Independence describes who performs the test, not what is being examined. A control owner can hand over genuine evidence, and an independent reviewer who collects only management statements has still gathered attestation.
distractors.C: Both forms can address a period or a point. A log covers a period continuously, and an attestation can be given about a single day; the period-versus-point distinction belongs to sampling design rather than to the nature of the item.
distractors.D: Tiering may change how much testing is proportionate, but it does not turn a claim into proof. A low-tier control tested only by attestation is untested; the organisation has simply decided it can live with not knowing.

explanation.concept: Test AI controls against artefacts the control produces, not statements about it. If operating the control leaves no trace an independent party can inspect, the control cannot be assured — and that absence of evidence is itself a design finding worth raising.
explanation.tip: Ask what the tester would look at. If the answer is a person's statement rather than a system-generated record, it is attestation whoever provides it.

topic: A closed postmortem action that did not prevent recurrence
stem: Nine months ago a Taiwanese semiconductor equipment maker's Claude-based service-report generator produced part numbers that did not exist, and field engineers ordered against them. The postmortem action — add a validation step that checks generated part numbers against the parts master — was implemented, tested and closed. The same failure has now recurred: the validation runs on the report's structured parts field, but the assistant also emits part numbers inside the free-text recommendations section, which is not validated. What should the second postmortem conclude about the governance process rather than about the defect?

options.text: The original action was implemented exactly as written, so this is a new defect rather than a recurrence and should be handled as a fresh incident with its own action.
The validation should move from the structured field to a check applied across the whole generated document, which would have caught both the original failure and this one.
Closure was verified against implementation rather than against whether the failure mode could still occur, so closure criteria have to test the failure mode, not the task.
Nine months is too long for a postmortem action to remain relevant, so actions should carry a review date at which their continued sufficiency is reconfirmed.

explanation.correct: Somebody wrote a task, somebody built the task, and somebody confirmed the task was built — and at no point did anyone ask whether an invented part number could still reach a field engineer. That is a defect in how actions are closed, and it generalises across every postmortem the organisation has ever run: any action closed on the same basis may have left its failure mode live. Closing against the failure mode would have meant attempting to reproduce the original incident after the fix and finding that the free-text path still worked.

distractors.A: Treating it as a new defect is the reasoning that produced the second incident. The failure mode is identical — a non-existent part number reaching an engineer who orders against it — and only the path through the document differs.
distractors.B: Whole-document validation is very likely the correct technical fix and should be in the action list. The stem asks what the process conclusion is, and adopting a better fix without changing how fixes are verified leaves the next action just as likely to be closed short.
distractors.D: An action review date would help where a fix degrades over time or the environment moves around it. This action never worked against the failure mode at all, so it was insufficient on the day it was closed rather than nine months later.

explanation.concept: Close a postmortem action against the failure mode, not against the task description. The verification question is whether the original incident could still happen, which usually means attempting to reproduce it after the fix rather than confirming that the change was made.
explanation.tip: When a stem says an action was implemented, tested and closed and the same failure returned, the finding is in the closure criteria. Options offering a better technical fix are answering a question the stem explicitly set aside.

topic: Contractual notification for a supplier's AI incident
stem: A Bulgarian online travel agency uses a supplied customer messaging platform whose AI reply-suggestion feature gave travellers incorrect refund-eligibility statements for three days. The agency learned of it from the vendor's public status page, four days after the vendor's own internal detection, and had to answer its customers with no account of what had happened. The contract covers security, availability and support; nothing addresses notification of AI behaviour failures. What should the agency require going forward?

options.text: A clause requiring the vendor to remediate any defect in the AI feature within a defined period, backed by service credits if that deadline is missed.
A right for the agency's internal audit function to audit the vendor's AI development, testing and release process annually, with findings shared between both parties.
A commitment that the vendor will not change the model behind the reply-suggestion feature without the agency's prior written consent on each occasion.
A notification clause with defined triggers, a maximum time from the vendor's own detection to notifying the agency, and a minimum content set for the notice.

explanation.correct: What the agency lacked was not a fix and not assurance — it was information, at a moment when its own customers were asking questions it could not answer. The clause has to close the specific gap the incident exposed: what kinds of behaviour failure oblige the vendor to speak, how long it may wait after its own detection rather than after public disclosure, and what the notice must contain so the agency can scope its own affected population. A status page is a broadcast; the agency needs a contractual obligation directed at it.

distractors.A: Remediation deadlines and credits govern how fast the vendor fixes its product and what it pays if it does not. Neither helps the agency tell travellers what happened, which is the exposure it actually carried for four days.
distractors.B: An annual audit right gives periodic assurance over the vendor's process and would not have produced a single word during those four days. It is a useful clause for a different purpose entirely.
distractors.C: Prior consent for model changes is a strong change-control provision and worth pursuing separately. It addresses planned changes; this incident was an unplanned defect in the existing feature, which no consent right would have surfaced.

explanation.concept: Vendor AI contracts need an incident notification clause distinct from change control and from remediation SLAs: what triggers notice, how long from the vendor's own detection, and what the notice must contain. Without it your first knowledge of a supplier's AI failure arrives at the same time as your customers'.
explanation.tip: Match the clause to the harm the stem describes. Here the harm was ignorance in front of customers, which narrows it to the option about being told.

topic: When an executive bypass counts as a valid risk acceptance
stem: An executive instructs a team to deploy an AI use case without the required governance review, saying they accept the risk personally. What makes that a legitimate risk acceptance rather than a bypass?

options.text: It is recorded as an exception describing the risk, with an expiry, and signed by the executive within their delegated authority.
It is reported to the governance board at its next meeting so that the board is aware the deployment has already taken place.
It is supported by a written statement from the team confirming that they raised the governance requirement before proceeding.
It is limited to a pilot population, keeping the exposure small enough for a single executive to carry personally.

explanation.correct: Risk acceptance is a real and necessary mechanism, and what separates it from a bypass is that it is written down, bounded, and made by someone whose delegation actually covers it. The record has to describe what risk is being accepted so the acceptance can be tested later; the expiry stops it becoming permanent; and the authority check is what makes it binding on the organisation rather than an individual's opinion. Take away any of the three and the deployment is simply proceeding without a decision anyone can point to.

distractors.B: Telling the board afterwards is disclosure, not authorisation. The board learns that something happened and has no decision in front of it, which is the difference between oversight and notification.
distractors.C: A note confirming that the team raised the requirement protects the team. It records that a bypass was knowing rather than accidental, which does nothing to make the bypass legitimate.
distractors.D: Scope limitation reduces exposure and is often a sensible condition to attach. It does not answer whether the executive holds the authority to accept this risk, and a pilot with real users can still cause real harm.

explanation.concept: A valid risk acceptance needs three things: a written description of the risk being accepted, an expiry, and a signature from someone whose delegated authority covers that level of risk. Missing the authority check is the most common defect and the one that invalidates the acceptance entirely.
explanation.tip: Test any claimed acceptance against the delegation framework first. Scope limits, disclosure and paper trails are useful additions to a valid acceptance and cannot substitute for one.

topic: External claim that overstates what the AI system does
stem: A Thai consumer lender's marketing site states that its Claude-based eligibility assistant 'checks your application against every one of our lending criteria before you submit'. The approved system card records that the assistant checks six of the eleven criteria and flags the remaining five for the applicant to confirm manually. The head of governance found the discrepancy while reviewing the site for an unrelated reason. Applications are running at about 3,000 a week. What should the head of governance do next?

options.text: Ask marketing to soften the wording at the next scheduled site update and record the discrepancy in the governance log for the quarterly report.
Have the claim corrected or removed now, and raise an incident so that the population who applied while it was live can be scoped.
Extend the assistant to check all eleven criteria so the published claim becomes accurate, and set a delivery date with the engineering team.
Refer the wording to legal for an opinion on whether it amounts to a misleading statement before any action is taken on the site.

explanation.correct: Applicants are relying on the claim right now, at 3,000 a week, and the reliance is the harm: someone who believes all eleven criteria were checked will not verify the five that were not, and will be declined for a reason the site told them had already been handled. That makes two things urgent and inseparable — stop the claim, and establish who acted on it while it was live. Raising it as an incident is what gets the second half done, because a marketing correction on its own leaves the affected population unexamined and unrecorded.

distractors.A: A scheduled update and a quarterly log entry treat an active misstatement as a housekeeping item. Thousands more applicants will rely on the claim before the next release, and the people already affected are never identified.
distractors.C: Making the claim true by building the missing checks is the trap. It is a multi-week engineering commitment during which the claim stays wrong, and it lets a marketing statement drive the product roadmap rather than the risk assessment.
distractors.D: Legal will need to be involved and their view will shape remedies and any disclosure. Waiting for an opinion before removing an inaccurate claim keeps the exposure open for no benefit, since removal is not the decision that needs legal analysis.

explanation.concept: External claims about what an AI system does are governed artefacts and must reconcile to the system card. When they diverge, correct the claim immediately and scope the population that relied on it — the reliance is the harm, and it does not stop when the wording is fixed.
explanation.tip: A stem that gives you a live volume is telling you the exposure is accumulating. That rules out every option whose first step is a scheduled update, a build, or an opinion.

topic: Content of a board escalation note on an AI incident
stem: A Ghanaian mobile money operator's Claude-based fraud triage assistant wrongly froze about 5,000 customer wallets for fourteen hours. The chief risk officer is writing a two-page note for the board, which meets in three days while the investigation is still open. Which THREE items must the note contain? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: What happened in plain terms, how many customers were affected, and what those customers actually experienced during the fourteen hours.
The prompt and model configuration in force at the time, so that the board can form its own view on whether the technical design was appropriate.
Whether the control environment failed as designed or was simply absent, and which specific control is being changed as a result.
What remains unknown at the time of writing, and the date by which the board will be told.
A comparison of the operator's AI incident rate against other mobile money providers, so the board can judge its relative performance.

explanation.correct: A board note during an open investigation has three jobs. It must establish the facts in terms a non-specialist director can hold — what happened, to how many people, and what those people experienced, since 5,000 frozen wallets means 5,000 people unable to transact. It must answer the board's real question, which is whether the control environment worked: a control that failed as designed and a control that was never there call for entirely different responses. And it must be explicit about what is not yet known and when it will be, because the alternative is a board that discovers the gaps by being surprised later.

distractors.B: Prompt and configuration detail is essential to the investigation and unusable by a board. Directors cannot assess a prompt, and including it invites a discussion of technical design in place of the oversight question the board is actually there to answer.
distractors.E: Peer incident rates are not reliably available, and constructing a comparison from what is would produce a number the operator cannot defend. It also reframes a control failure as a benchmarking exercise, which is the wrong conversation for an audit or risk discussion.

explanation.concept: A board incident note covers facts and customer impact, whether the control environment failed or was absent and what is changing, and the open questions with a date. Technical configuration and peer comparisons belong elsewhere; the board is assessing oversight, not design.
explanation.tip: In board-communication items, test each option against what a director can act on. Anything requiring specialist interpretation, or any comparison built on data you do not have, is a distractor.

topic: AI policy scope that omits employee-affecting decisions
stem: A Sri Lankan apparel manufacturer's HR team has begun using a Claude assistant to score internal promotion applications against the company's competency framework. The scores are printed in the promotion panel's pack, and the panel says it treats them as one input among several. The company's AI policy requires customer-affecting AI to be registered, tiered and given a named owner, and is silent on employee-affecting AI. What is the correct governance position?

options.text: The policy is silent on employee-affecting AI, so registration is not required; the HR team should record the assistant in its own procedure manual and in the promotion panel's terms of reference.
The scores should be removed from the panel pack altogether, because a panel that has seen a numeric score cannot genuinely treat it as one input among several.
The practice is acceptable provided the panel records its reasons whenever it departs from a score, which evidences that independent judgement was exercised in each case.
Employee-affecting decisions carry the same accountability requirements as customer-affecting ones; the policy's scope is the defect, and this use must be registered, tiered and owned.

explanation.correct: A promotion decision determines someone's pay, standing and career, and the person affected has no more insight into how a score was produced than a customer would. Nothing about the accountability requirement — a named owner, a risk tier, an evaluation of whether the scoring reflects the competency framework, a route to challenge — depends on which side of the employment relationship the affected person sits. The silence in the policy is a scope defect that this use case has exposed, and reading silence as permission is how organisations end up with their least-scrutinised AI operating on their own staff.

distractors.A: Treating an unaddressed category as permitted inverts the policy's purpose, and local documentation inside HR gives no owner, no tier and no visibility to anyone reviewing the estate. It also leaves the next employee-affecting use case in exactly the same position.
distractors.B: Anchoring on a displayed score is a genuine concern and may well be a control the assessment recommends. Removing the score answers a question about panel design while leaving the use unregistered, unowned and unevaluated.
distractors.C: Recording departures produces useful evidence and is a reasonable condition. As the whole answer it accepts the use without anyone having assessed whether the scoring is sound, and it makes the panel's paperwork the only control.

explanation.concept: AI policy scope should be defined by whose interests a decision affects, not by whether that person is a customer. Employee-affecting AI — hiring, promotion, performance, scheduling, discipline — needs the same registration, tiering and named accountability as customer-facing systems.
explanation.tip: When a stem tells you the policy is silent on the exact category in play, the silence is the item. Options that reason from the gap rather than about it are distractors.

topic: What makes each step of an autonomy ladder a real gate
stem: A responsible scaling approach grants an AI system permissions in graduated steps — suggest, then act with confirmation, then act autonomously — rather than all at once. What does each step need in order to function as a gate?

options.text: A longer observation period than the step before it, so that rarer failure modes have time to appear under production conditions.
A separate approval from the governance board, so that no single team can advance a system through the ladder unchallenged.
A pre-agreed measure of whether the previous step performed acceptably, and a stated threshold that has to be met before advancing.
A distinct system card version, so that the deployed configuration at each level of autonomy is separately documented and signed.

explanation.correct: A gate is something that can be failed. Without a measure agreed before the step began and a threshold stated in advance, advancement is decided by whether anyone objects — and after weeks of a system running without visible disaster, nobody does. The measure has to be specific to what the step was testing: at 'act with confirmation', the useful number is how often the human declined to confirm and why, because that is the direct evidence about whether removing confirmation is safe. Everything else in the ladder is scaffolding around that judgement.

distractors.A: Duration is a proxy for exposure and a poor one on its own. A longer period at low traffic may generate fewer opportunities to fail than a short one at high volume, and time elapsed says nothing about how the system performed while it passed.
distractors.B: Board approval at each step adds independence and slows self-advancement, which is worth having for high-tier systems. The board still needs a criterion to decide against; without one it is applying judgement to the same absence of evidence the team had.
distractors.D: Versioned cards keep the documentation honest as autonomy changes and should be produced. Documentation records what was decided; it does not supply the basis on which the decision should have been taken.

explanation.concept: Graduated autonomy is only a control when each step carries a pre-agreed success measure and threshold. Define what evidence the step must produce before it starts, and make advancement conditional on the evidence rather than on the absence of complaints.
explanation.tip: Ask what would cause the step to be failed. If nothing in the option could produce a 'no', it is process around the gate rather than the gate itself.

topic: Responding to a programme exempted from AI approval
stem: A French luxury goods group's executive committee has exempted a flagship AI-first customer experience programme, covering seven customer-facing use cases, from the group's AI approval process for twelve months 'so the programme can move at pace', directing the governance team to review the outputs retrospectively at the end. The group risk framework permits the executive committee to accept risk within its delegated authority provided acceptances are recorded. The head of AI governance must respond. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Convert the decision into a recorded exception: named accepting executive, scope limited to the seven use cases, compensating controls, a shorter expiry, and defined stop conditions.
Decline to operate the exemption on the grounds that the approval process is mandated by the group risk framework, and escalate the matter to the board's risk committee.

Continue reviewing the programme informally and without decision rights, circulating observations to the programme's steering group, so that some governance visibility over the seven use cases is retained.
Accept the retrospective review as directed, but require the programme to produce system cards for all seven use cases so the eventual review has material to work with.

explanation.correct: The framework lets the executive committee accept this risk, so the governance head is not being asked to permit something impermissible — they are being handed an acceptance that was made in the wrong form. Every defect is in the shape of the decision rather than its substance: no individual named as accepting, no boundary on what the exemption covers as the programme grows, nothing reducing the risk in the meantime, twelve months with no review point, and no condition under which it stops early. Reconstituting it as a proper exception preserves the committee's authority while restoring every property that makes an acceptance governable.

distractors.B: Refusal misreads the framework, which explicitly permits this committee to accept risk within its delegation. Escalating over a decision the body was entitled to make spends the governance function's credibility on the wrong argument and leaves the exemption unbounded while the dispute runs.
distractors.C: Shadow review without decision rights is the least defensible position available: it consumes governance effort, produces observations nobody must act on, and creates a record implying oversight that did not exist. It is worse than a clean, recorded exception.
distractors.D: System cards are worth requiring and would improve the retrospective review. Twelve months of unassessed customer-facing deployment still passes with no stop condition, and a card written to support a review after the fact is documentation rather than control.

explanation.concept: When an authorised body decides to bypass a control, the governance response is to convert the decision into a properly formed risk acceptance — named accepter, bounded scope, compensating controls, expiry, stop conditions — rather than to refuse it or to shadow it. Governance shapes acceptances it cannot prevent.
explanation.tip: Check whether the stem grants the decision-maker authority. If it does, options that refuse or escalate are wrong; if it does not, they become the answer.

topic: Turning one-off shadow AI discovery into a standing control
stem: An Estonian online gaming company ran a shadow AI discovery exercise last year: four weeks of analysis across finance, identity and network data, producing thirty-one findings, all since registered or retired. The company already requires AI registration at project inception and at supplier onboarding. A spot check now finds twelve new unregistered uses — six browser-based tools adopted by individuals and six developer API keys — every one of which bypassed both registration points. The security lead proposes repeating the four-week exercise annually. What is the better design?

options.text: Repeat the exercise every six months rather than annually, halving the window in which new unregistered use can accumulate before anyone looks.
Turn the discovery queries into scheduled jobs that run continuously and raise a case whenever a new AI signal appears that does not reconcile to the register.
Strengthen registration at project inception and supplier onboarding, so that new use is caught as it is created rather than found months afterwards.
Target the next exercise at the business units that produced most of last year's findings, since unregistered use tends to concentrate where it was previously found.

explanation.correct: The expensive part of the original exercise was working out which signals matter and how to join them; that analysis is done and can be automated. Running it continuously turns a periodic project into a control that produces a case the moment a signal fails to reconcile, which is the only design that keeps pace with individuals installing tools and developers adding keys. The stem also rules out the alternative that would otherwise be strongest: registration gates already exist at both inception and onboarding, and all twelve new uses went around them, because neither gate sits in the path of a browser install or a personal API key.

distractors.A: Six-monthly sweeps still leave months of accumulation and still consume four weeks of effort each time. The cadence changes the size of the backlog discovered, not the fact that discovery happens long after adoption.
distractors.C: Registration at inception and onboarding is exactly what the company already has, and the stem states that all twelve uses bypassed both. Strengthening a gate that these adoption routes never pass through cannot catch them.
distractors.D: Targeting last year's hotspots optimises for where the problem was, and the twelve new uses split evenly between individual tool adoption and developer keys — populations that are spread across the company rather than concentrated in a unit.

explanation.concept: Shadow AI discovery should be a standing reconciliation, not a periodic project: automate the signal queries, run them continuously, and raise a case on anything that does not match the register. Registration gates catch use that passes through a formal process; continuous discovery catches the use that never does.
explanation.tip: When a stem says the existing preventive gates were all bypassed, options that strengthen those gates are eliminated on the facts, however sound they are in general.

topic: Governance status of a pilot AI deployment
stem: For governance purposes, how should an AI pilot that serves real users be treated?

options.text: As an experiment running on historical or synthetic data, distinguishable from production by the fact that no live decision anywhere depends on what it produces.
As a time-boxed activity with a go or no-go decision at its end, which is what separates it from a deployment that simply runs until somebody decides to stop it.
As affecting real people and therefore requiring the same controls as production, scoped to a smaller population; the label does not reduce the obligations.
As exempt from registration until it is proposed for production, at which point it enters the inventory with its pilot results attached.

explanation.correct: A pilot that serves real users produces real outcomes for them, and none of those people experiences the harm as provisional. The word describes the organisation's intent to learn and to decide later; it says nothing about the exposure the users are carrying meanwhile. So the controls owe them the same protections — registration, an accountable owner, an oversight arrangement, an incident route, a way to complain — with scope and duration bounded rather than obligations reduced. Treating pilot status as a discount is one of the most common ways unassessed systems reach the public.

distractors.A: This describes an offline experiment, which genuinely does attract lighter controls because nobody outside the team is exposed. The distinction is whether real users are affected, and the stem places this pilot on the other side of that line.
distractors.B: Time-boxing and an end decision are real and useful properties of a well-run pilot, and their absence is a common defect. They describe how the pilot is managed rather than what protections the people it touches are owed.
distractors.D: Deferring registration until production means the inventory omits systems that are live with real users, which defeats the purpose of holding one. It is also the point at which a pilot most needs an owner, because nobody has yet been assigned long-term responsibility.

explanation.concept: Pilot is a statement about duration and intent, not about risk. If real people are affected, apply production controls scoped to the smaller population — registration, named owner, oversight, incident route — and use the time box to bound exposure rather than to defer obligations.
explanation.tip: Whenever a stem attaches a softening label — pilot, experiment, proof of concept, internal trial — check whether real users are affected. If they are, the label changes nothing.

topic: Register fields that support downstream governance processes
stem: A Bangladeshi garment exporter's AI register currently holds system name, accountable owner, business unit, model and go-live date. Three downstream processes need to run from it: the annual assurance plan, which selects what to test; the incident triage desk, which sets response urgency; and the board coverage report. None of the three can currently be produced from the register. Which TWO fields should be added? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The risk tier, derived from the severity of the consequence if the output is wrong and whether output is acted on without human review.
A free-text description of the model's known limitations, copied from the provider's published documentation for that model.
The classes of data the system processes and the source systems those classes come from.
The name of the engineer who most recently changed the system's prompts or its runtime configuration.
The projected annual cost of running the system, so that the register also supports technology budget planning.

explanation.correct: Both fields feed all three consumers, which is the test the stem sets. Risk tier tells the assurance plan what to test and how deeply, tells triage how fast to respond when something involving that system is reported, and gives the board a coverage view expressed in terms of exposure rather than system count. Data classes and their sources tell assurance what scope a test has to cover, tell triage immediately whether an incident touches worker or customer records, and let the board see where the organisation's sensitive data is being processed by AI. Neither can be reconstructed from name, owner, unit, model and date.

distractors.B: Provider limitation text is generic to the model and identical across every entry using it, so it distinguishes nothing between systems. It also describes the model rather than the deployment, which is where the exporter's risk actually sits.
distractors.D: The most recent change author belongs in version control, where it is captured automatically and stays accurate. In a register it is stale within days and serves none of the three processes named.
distractors.E: Cost supports budgeting, which is a fourth process the stem did not ask about. It tells assurance nothing about what to test, triage nothing about urgency, and the board nothing about coverage.

explanation.concept: Design inventory fields backwards from the processes that consume the register. Risk tier and data classes are the two that almost every downstream consumer needs; fields that serve only one process, or that duplicate a system of record like version control, add maintenance burden without adding decisions.
explanation.tip: In field-selection items, test each candidate against every consumer the stem names. The keys are usually the fields that serve all of them; single-purpose fields are the distractors.

topic: Risk acceptance signed outside the delegation framework
stem: Internal audit at a Latvian digital identity provider finds that a high-tier AI use case — automated identity document verification — went live under a risk acceptance signed by a delivery manager. The firm's delegation framework places acceptance of high-tier AI risk with the executive risk committee. The system has been live for seven months and has processed 1.2 million verifications with no identified harm. What should the head of internal audit do next?

options.text: Recommend that the delegation framework be revised so delivery managers may accept high-tier AI risk where the executive risk committee cannot be convened in time.
Report the finding in the next scheduled audit report, given that the system operates normally and no harm has been identified across seven months of use.
Require the system to be withdrawn from service immediately, since it has run for seven months without a valid risk acceptance under the framework.
Escalate to the executive risk committee now so the body with authority decides on current evidence, and record the invalid acceptance as a control finding in its own right.

explanation.correct: There are two distinct problems and the response has to address both. Substantively, a high-tier system is running with no valid acceptance behind it, and only the executive risk committee can cure that — by accepting, requiring mitigation, or withdrawing it, on the evidence that now exists including seven months of operating history. Procedurally, an acceptance was signed outside the delegation framework, which means the framework is not being applied and this is unlikely to be the only instance. Audit's job is to put the decision in front of the right body and to raise the control failure separately, not to take the decision itself.

distractors.A: Amending the framework to legitimise what happened removes the finding by lowering the standard. Delegation thresholds exist because high-tier risk should be accepted by people with the standing to carry it; convening difficulty is an argument for a faster escalation route, not a lower one.
distractors.B: Waiting for the reporting cycle applies routine handling to a high-tier system operating without valid authorisation. The absence of identified harm over seven months is reassuring and not the same as evidence of safety, particularly where nobody has assessed what to look for.
distractors.C: Withdrawal may be what the committee decides, but internal audit does not hold that decision. Pre-empting it also disrupts an identity verification service on procedural grounds without the business impact having been weighed by anyone entitled to weigh it.

explanation.concept: When a risk acceptance is found to have been signed outside the delegation framework, escalate the underlying decision to the body that holds the authority and raise the invalid acceptance as a separate control finding. Assurance functions surface decisions to the right owner; they do not substitute for that owner.
explanation.tip: Split the item into the substantive risk and the process breach — well-formed answers here address both. Options that only fix one, or that have audit make the business decision, are the distractors.

topic: AI used inside the internal audit function itself
stem: An Icelandic pension fund's internal audit team has started using a Claude assistant to read AI system documentation and draft audit findings. The audit committee asks the chief audit executive whether this compromises the function's independence or the reliability of its opinions. What is the correct position?

options.text: Audit's use is a registered use case like any other, the auditor remains accountable for every finding issued, and the assistant itself must be reviewed by someone outside audit.
Internal audit should not use AI to produce findings at all, because a finding produced with machine assistance cannot be defended as the auditor's own independent professional judgement.
The use needs no registration, because internal audit is an independent function whose tools are governed by its own methodology and quality standards rather than by the group AI policy.
The use is acceptable provided each report states which findings were AI-assisted, so that the audit committee can weigh those findings differently from the ones produced unaided.

explanation.correct: Three things hold at once. The assurance function is not exempt from the organisation's AI policy, and exempting it would be a poor look for a function that tests other people's compliance with the same policy. Accountability for a finding stays with the auditor who signs it, regardless of what helped draft it, exactly as it would for a junior's draft. And there is a genuine self-review threat: audit cannot be the reviewer of the tool its own opinions now depend on, so the assistant needs assurance from outside the function.

distractors.B: This would rule out most drafting aids auditors already use. The standard is whether the auditor exercised and can defend their own judgement on the finding, not whether every word was typed unaided, and a blanket prohibition is not the position the audit committee needs.
distractors.C: Claiming exemption on the basis of independence is the weakest available answer. Independence governs who audit reports to and how it forms opinions; it does not remove the function from group policies on data handling and AI use, and asserting otherwise undermines audit's standing to test those policies elsewhere.
distractors.D: Labelling findings as AI-assisted invites the committee to discount them, which either devalues sound findings or creates pressure to avoid the label. Every finding should carry the same weight because every finding is signed by an auditor who stands behind it.

explanation.concept: Assurance functions are subject to the AI policy they help enforce. Register the use, keep accountability for the opinion with the named auditor, and arrange independent review of any tool the function's own conclusions depend on — the self-review threat is the specific issue AI use creates for audit.
explanation.tip: When a function argues it is exempt because it is independent, that is the distractor. Independence describes reporting lines, not immunity from the organisation's own controls.
